phonemes.desc: Short open vowel [a], the first syllable of the Latin word for breath and soul.
Short [nɪ], with the vowel reduced and unstressed in Classical Latin.
Short [ma], the feminine noun ending that gives the word its grammatical form.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AH-nih-mah' — stress the first syllable; the middle vowel is short and light.
pronunciation.note: Anima is a Latin word, not a Greek proper name. It has no indigenous alphabetic 'original script' other than the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form anima is already the Latin spelling; the restoration capitalises the proper-noun form as a scholarly citation. Because no distinctive diacritic or special letter is added, the entry is Tier 2.

domains.title: The Breath that Becomes Soul
domains.subtitle: Soul, Breath, and Life Force
domains.lead: Anima is the Latin word for breath, air, and — by extension — the soul or life-force that animates a living body. It names one of the most ancient equations in Western thought: that the difference between a corpse and a living person is the presence of breath. From this simple observation Latin developed a rich vocabulary of animation, soul, and spirit that still shapes modern psychology, religion, and biology.

cards.name: Breath
cards.desc: The literal meaning of anima: the air drawn in and expelled by living creatures.

cards.name: Soul
cards.desc: In philosophy and theology anima becomes the immaterial principle that gives life and, later, the rational soul.

cards.name: Life Force
cards.desc: The active power that distinguishes the living from the dead, the moving from the still.

cards.name: Inspiration
cards.desc: Literally 'breathing in' — the moment when life, ideas, or the divine enter the self.

symbols.name: Breath or wind
symbols.meaning: The invisible current that enters at birth and departs at death.

symbols.name: Bird
symbols.meaning: A widespread symbol for the soul as something light, winged, and capable of leaving the body.

symbols.name: Blood or pulse
symbols.meaning: The physiological sign that anima is at work in the living body.

symbols.name: Flame
symbols.meaning: The small fire of individual life, easily extinguished and often identified with the soul's spark.

mythology.lead: Anima is not a mythological character in the Greek or Roman sense; it is a concept that acquired a long philosophical and theological history. Its 'mythology' is therefore the story of how breath became soul, and how soul became one of the foundation stones of Western psychology.

myths.title: The Breath of Life
myths.text: In Classical Latin anima first means breath, air, or breeze. Cicero uses it for the vital breath that sustains life, and Lucretius describes the soul as a subtle, airy stuff mixed with blood and heat, dispersed at death. The word thus begins as a physical fact and only gradually becomes a metaphysical principle.

myths.title: The Rational Soul
myths.text: Early Latin Christianity adopted anima as the standard translation for Greek psychē and Hebrew nephesh. Augustine's *De anima* and later scholastic treatises made the anima rationalis the immortal, thinking part of the human person, created by God and destined for salvation or damnation.

myths.title: Jung's Anima
myths.text: In C. G. Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine image in the male psyche, the soul-figure that mediates between the ego and the unconscious. The term preserves the Latin sense of soul while giving it a new, psychological meaning: the anima is not a metaphysical substance but an inner figure shaped by culture and personal history.

myths.title: Animation and Life
myths.text: English words such as animal, animate, animation, and equanimity all descend from anima. Each preserves a different shade of the original meaning: the living, the moving, the inspired, and the balanced soul. The word has travelled from biology to cinema without ever fully losing its connection to breath.

syncretism: The Latin anima overlaps with Greek psychē, Hebrew nephesh, Sanskrit ātman, and Greek pneuma. All of these terms begin with breath or wind and develop into concepts of soul, spirit, or self. In medieval philosophy anima became the bridge between Aristotelian biology and Christian theology, a development that shaped European thought until the early modern period. In modern psychology it survives as Jung's anima and as the root of 'animation,' the art of giving apparent life to images.
culturalLegacy: Anima is one of the most quietly influential words in Western languages. It underlies 'animal' (a being that has breath), 'animate' (to give life), 'animation' (the illusion of life in images), and 'animism' (the attribution of soul to natural objects). In Jungian psychology the anima is a central archetype, and in contemporary spirituality it names the feminine soul-principle. The word's persistence shows that the ancient equation of breath with life has never really been replaced.
extendedMeditation:
To meditate on Anima is to meditate on the boundary between body and whatever we call the self. Breath is the one physiological process that can be voluntary or automatic; it links the conscious will to the autonomic body. The Latin word reminds us that the soul was not originally imagined as a ghost in a machine but as the very fact of being alive.

In a digital age, when consciousness is often modelled as computation, Anima asks a simpler question: what is it that makes a living thing living? The answer may not be a substance but a process — the continuous exchange of inner and outer, self and world, that breath so perfectly symbolizes.
originalScriptNote: Anima is a Latin word. It has no 'original script' in the sense of Greek or cuneiform; its canonical form is the Latin spelling anima. The ASCII form anima already represents the Latin spelling exactly. The restoration Anima is therefore the capitalised proper-noun citation form, not a phonetic recovery. The appropriate label is 'Scholarly Transliteration' or simply 'Latin'.
